name: Question 5
problem:
$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-6x{y}^{′}+10y=-2{x}^{3}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{5}+B{x}^{2},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{3}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2})^{′}=2x, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(2x)^{′}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
{x}^{2}(2)-6x(2x)+10({x}^{2})=-2{x}^{3}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{2}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{3},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{3})^{′}=3{x}^{2}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(3{x}^{2})^{′}=6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
{x}^{2}(6x)-6x(3{x}^{2})+10({x}^{3})=-2{x}^{3}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={x}^{3}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{x}^{5}+B{x}^{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{x}^{5}+B{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=x2, we have y′(x)=(x2)′=2x,y″(x)=(2x)′=2. Substituting this into the equation, we have x2(2)−6x(2x)+10(x2)=−2x3.× So, yp(x)=x2 isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.
  • For yp(x)=x3, we have y′(x)=(x3)′=3x2,y″(x)=(3x2)′=6x. Substituting this into the equation, we have x2(6x)−6x(3x2)+10(x3)=−2x3.✓ So, yp(x)=x3 is a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Ax5+Bx2. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Ax5+Bx2+x3 where A and B are arbitrary constants.
